strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: representing each token as a vector of negative squared distances to all vocabulary embeddings yields a forward process that progressively dissolves semantic information while retaining a natural argmax-style decoding path, addressing a genuine weakness of both Gaussian-embedding and simplex-based text diffusion.

Appendix C gives a crisp, correct argument that simplex diffusion (SSD-LM/TESS) is a special case of the proposed distance-based latent space under the trivial metric, which both positions the contribution theoretically and makes the empirical simplex-vs-SMOOTHIE comparison meaningful.
Theorem 4.1 (MSE on D0 is optimal-prediction-equivalent to MSE on embeddings, up to a constant) is a useful practical simplification, and the proof in Appendix D is sound and self-contained.

The controlled latent-space comparison (embedding vs. simplex vs. SMOOTHIE) with identical architecture, hyperparameters, and decoding is a methodological strength often missing in this literature; the finding that architecture choice matters as much as diffusion space (simplex⋆ beating TESS on Quasar-T) is honestly reported.

Experiments span four seq2seq tasks with established baselines and metrics, hyperparameters and dataset statistics are fully reported (Appendix E/G), ablations on δ̃, denoising steps, and the decoder are included, and the limitations (pre-trained frozen embeddings, fixed sequence length) are candidly discussed.
Efficiency claim is concrete and supported: SMOOTHIE achieves the best mean rank while requiring 2-10x fewer denoising steps than competing diffusion methods (Table 5, Table 6).
weaknesses: The headline claim that SMOOTHIE 'outperforms existing diffusion-based models in generation quality' is only partially supported. On Quasar-T the re-implemented simplex variant beats SMOOTHIE (BS 63.0 vs 62.4, BLEU 19.5 vs 19.0); on Newsela-Auto, SeqDiffuSeq and DiffuSeq clearly beat it (BS 82.1/79.1 vs 73.7, BLEU 37.1/29.9 vs 19.9); and BART beats SMOOTHIE on nearly every task. The mean-rank summary (Table 5) omits XSum and these losses dilute the contribution's empirical significance.

No variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for any table; several margins (e.g., SMOOTHIE 62.4 vs Simplex 63.0, or Embedding vs SMOOTHIE on Quasar-T) are small enough that single-run results could flip rankings.

The actual model input is ptE, a d-dimensional weighted average of embeddings - the same functional form as embedding-based diffusion. The distance-based latent therefore only affects the kernel weighting of the softmax, and the paper does not isolate or explain mechanistically why this particular Nadaraya-Watson weighting helps beyond intuition and Figure 1; a deeper analysis (e.g., of the noised distributions or token confusion patterns) is missing.

Comparisons with prior work mix results taken from other papers (marked ⋄, sometimes under different training/evaluation setups) with the authors' re-implementations (⋆), complicating interpretation; recent competitive discrete/masked diffusion methods (e.g., SEDD [31], which is cited but not compared) are absent from the baseline set.

Because D0 is an m×V matrix (V = BERT vocabulary, ~30k), the computational cost and memory implications of the distance representation are not discussed or measured, particularly relative to the k-logit simplex alternative.

Evaluation is exclusively automatic metrics; no human evaluation is provided, which matters given that BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore can favor lexically conservative outputs, and the δ̃ analysis shows the method can trade diversity for quality.

Minor presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract is truncated/incomplete ('available at'), Theorem 4.1 implicitly assumes the model class can realize both optimal predictions (universality assumption unstated), and the derivation of the variational bound for the non-Markovian forward process (Eq. 6 uses q(Dt-1|D0)) deserves a sentence justifying its validity, following the DDPM/DDIM non-Markovian analysis.

strengths: The core idea is conceptually clean: representing tokens by vectors of negative squared Euclidean distances to all vocabulary embeddings and diffusing in this space is an elegant generalization of simplex diffusion (SSD-LM/TESS), and Appendix C gives a correct and simple proof that the simplex latent space is a special case under the trivial metric.

The connection to blurring/heat-dissipation diffusion in vision (Hoogeboom & Salimans; Rissanen et al.) is a sensible and well-motivated transfer of ideas to discrete data, and the Nadaraya-Watson interpretation of the softmax input is insightful.

The paper is honest about its design trade-offs in places, e.g., the decoder ablation (Table 8) showing that a complex decoder does not help, and the candid discussion that simplex diffusion with their architecture actually beats SMOOTHIE on Quasar-T.

The controlled ablation (Embedding*/Simplex*/SMOOTHIE* trained under identical architecture, hyperparameters, and decoding) is the right experimental design for isolating the effect of the latent space, and hyperparameters and compute details are reported (Appendix E).
weaknesses: The central claim that SMOOTHIE outperforms existing diffusion-based models is overstated relative to the evidence: on Quasar-T their own fair re-implementation of simplex diffusion beats SMOOTHIE, and on Newsela-Auto both DiffuSeq and SeqDiffuSeq clearly outperform it (Table 4). The mean-rank argument (Table 5) mixes SMOOTHIE's numbers with results copied from prior papers whose models use different architectures, which the authors themselves concede matters ('choosing the right model architecture is no less important than choosing the right diffusion space'). This undercuts the paper's main empirical conclusion.

The baseline set is dated and omits the strongest recent discrete diffusion models (e.g., SEDD, MDLM-style masking diffusion, DiffusionBERT successors); the comparison is largely against 2021-2023 methods, so 'outperforms existing diffusion-based models' is not established against the current state of the art.

No statistical significance testing, error bars, or human evaluation is provided. Many headline gaps (e.g., BERTScore 62.4 vs 63.0 vs 62.0 on Quasar-T; 68.0 vs 65.6 on XSum) are small and could fall within run-to-run variance, yet the paper draws conclusions like 'the distance-based latent space clearly outperforms' from single runs.

The method relies on a fixed, non-contextual pre-trained BERT embedding matrix, which is in tension with the paper's motivation via the 'Euclidean semantic space hypothesis' (word embeddings as metric recovery) and with TEncDM's finding that context-dependent embeddings are better diffusion latents. The limitation is acknowledged, but it caps the plausibility of the semantic-smoothing story, and no ablation over embedding sources (e.g., trainable vs frozen, different encoders) is provided.

Theorem 4.1 is technically trivial (a first-moment argument plus softmax shift invariance) and its practical significance is thin; the paper also switches to a simplified loss (dropping the 2\tilde{delta}^2 sigma_t^4 scaling) whose theoretical justification is not discussed. Similarly, key hyperparameters (tilde-delta chosen via one ROCStories experiment, sigma schedule constants) are tuned empirically with limited analysis.

Presentation issues reduce confidence: the code URL is missing from the abstract, there are numerous typos and grammatical errors throughout ('minumum', 'each of other text diffusion approaches', 'Hyperparemeter', 'complex decoder do not affect', 'does not operate directly on these distribution'), and the inconsistent mixing of results taken from prior work vs. re-implementations (marked with symbols) makes Tables 2-4 hard to interpret.

Several methodological choices are ad hoc and weaken reproducibility/generalization claims: 500 denoising steps only for Newsela-Auto, discarding tokens past EOS to emulate variable lengths, no clamping or classifier-free guidance based on qualitative judgments, and the decision to exclude self-conditioning from other datasets based on a single-dataset cost/benefit analysis.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely interesting: representing tokens by vectors of (negative squared) Euclidean distances to all vocabulary embeddings yields a diffusion process that smoothly interpolates between semantic similarity structure (like embedding diffusion) and natural argmax decoding (like simplex diffusion). The claim that simplex diffusion is a special case under the trivial metric is proven cleanly in Appendix C, which strengthens the framing of the method as a generalization.

The paper includes a well-designed controlled comparison: embedding, simplex, and distance-based latent spaces are trained with the same architecture, hyperparameters, and decoding strategy, isolating the effect of the diffusion space. This is more rigorous than typical comparisons against numbers copied from prior papers.

Useful ablations are provided: the effect of the reverse noise variance δ̃ (fluency/diversity trade-off, Fig. 2), the number of denoising steps (Table 6), the decoder ablation (Table 8), and self-conditioning (Table 3). The finding that a complex decoder is unnecessary for their latent space is an interesting and practically relevant result.
Theorem 4.1 (equivalence of predicting distances vs. predicting embeddings under MSE, given softmax-invariant inputs) is a correct and helpful observation, with a complete proof in Appendix D.

Reproducibility is reasonably good: full hyperparameter tables (Table 7), dataset statistics, training details, and a stated code release. The limitations section is honest and substantive (fixed pre-trained BERT embeddings, fixed sequence length), and a societal impact statement is included.
weaknesses: The headline empirical claim ('SMOOTHIE outperforms existing diffusion-based models on the majority of tasks') is weaker than it sounds. In the paper's own controlled comparisons, the re-implemented simplex baseline beats SMOOTHIE on Quasar-T (BS 63.0 vs 62.4, BLEU 19.5 vs 19.0), and DiffuSeq/SeqDiffuSeq clearly beat it on Newsela-Auto (BS 82.1/79.1 vs 73.7; BLEU 37.1 vs 19.9). SMOOTHIE wins decisively only on XSum and QQP. The mean-rank analysis (Table 5) covers only 3 of 4 datasets and an ad hoc average of two metrics, without statistical significance testing or variance across seeds, and many margins are small.

Notable recent baselines are missing. For a 2026 main-track submission on text diffusion, comparisons against strong recent discrete/semi-autoregressive diffusion models (e.g., score-entropy discrete diffusion, masked diffusion LMs such as MDLM/SED-era methods, Plaid) are absent; the diffusion baselines are largely 2022–2023 methods. This limits the evidence that the proposed latent space is competitive with the current state of the art.

There remains a large gap to autoregressive baselines (BART and FLAN-T5 outperform SMOOTHIE on nearly every task), and the paper does not clearly articulate what practical scenario would favor this method over strong AR models; the motivation rests on the design-space argument in Table 1 rather than demonstrated practical advantage.

Several methodological details are under-justified. The forward process is non-Markovian with a constant noise variance δ and signal decay 1/σ_t², and the reverse process uses a different variance δ̃; the ELBO derivation (Eqs. 5–9) treats these choices somewhat loosely, and the sensitivity to σ_min/σ_max/d and δ (only δ̃ is ablated) is not studied. The noise scheduler constants (σ_min=1.5, σ_max=200, d=9) appear hand-tuned without justification.

The latent dimensionality scales with vocabulary size (V ≈ 30k for BERT), so D_0 is a sequence-length × V matrix; the paper argues the model actually consumes p_t E (lower-dimensional), but the softmax over ~30k noisy logits and the memory/compute implications of the distance matrix are not analyzed, and the method's applicability to larger vocabularies or subword settings is not discussed.

Presentation has noticeable flaws: grammatical errors throughout (e.g., 'which respect discreteness', 'can not be directly applied', 'hyperparemeters'), mixed sourcing of baseline numbers (some copied from prior papers, some re-implemented) makes tables hard to compare despite the symbol conventions, and Table 2 omits BLEU/diversity metrics reported for other datasets.
The unconditional generation evaluation (Fig. 2) uses a single dataset and no baselines, so the fluency/diversity control claimed as a contribution is demonstrated only in isolation.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: representing each token as a vector of negative squared Euclidean distances to all vocabulary embeddings, then diffusing this representation, yields a forward process that both preserves a natural decoding path (argmax over distances) and incorporates semantic structure via a Nadaraya-Watson/Gaussian-kernel smoothing. The connection to the image-domain blurring/heat-dissipation line (Rissanen et al., 2023; Hoogeboom & Salimans, 2023) is a sensible and well-explained transfer.

Appendix A provides a crisp proof that simplex-based diffusion (SSD-LM, TESS) is a special case of the proposed distance-based latent space under the trivial metric, which usefully unifies prior approaches and frames the method as a generalization rather than an ad hoc alternative.

Theorem 4.1 (predicting embeddings is equivalent to predicting the distance matrix up to a softmax-invariant shift) is a nice, simple result that justifies a low-dimensional MSE training objective instead of the high-variance V-dimensional one, and the proof in Appendix C is correct.

The empirical study is unusually thorough for this area: five datasets spanning unconditional and seq2seq generation, a broad set of diffusion and autoregressive baselines, and a carefully controlled ablation where the embedding- and simplex-based latent spaces are re-trained under identical architecture, hyperparameters, and decoding, isolating the effect of the diffusion space. Additional ablations cover embedding choice (BERT vs. GPT-2 vs. GloVe), the noise scheduler parameter d, self-conditioning, δ̃, number of denoising steps, and solver choice.

The computation-matched comparison (giving embedding diffusion 1.75× more steps to offset its lower per-step cost) is a fair-dealing detail often missing from similar papers, and generation time/memory are honestly reported (Table 2).

The limitations section is candid and substantive: reliance on frozen pretrained embeddings (with a credible discussion of why end-to-end training is unstable), and the O(seq len × d × V) distance-computation bottleneck with an honest explanation of why top-k approximations fail.
Qualitative semantic-degradation examples (Table 13) concretely illustrate the claimed advantage of the forward process over simplex noising.
weaknesses: The theoretical treatment is heuristic. The forward process is non-Markovian with a δ-independent variance, and the reverse process uses a different variance δ̃ (following Rissanen et al., 2023), so the derived ELBO does not correspond to a consistent generative model of the data distribution; the prior p(DT)=N(0, δ̃²I) does not match the forward marginal q(DT|D0). This is common in practice but the paper presents Eq. 6 as a variational bound without discussing this gap.

Theorem 4.1 only establishes equivalence of the two training targets for optimal predictors under the conditional expectation; for the suboptimal fθ actually trained, D0(fθ) and gθ need not coincide, yet Eq. 9 uses the equivalence in the sampling scheme without quantifying the approximation error. Similarly, the explanation of why the proposed solver beats DDPM/DDIM (Table 6) is admittedly speculative ('a deeper theoretical understanding remains an open question').

Improvements over the strongest controlled baselines are marginal on several tasks: on Quasar-T, SMOOTHIE essentially ties Simplex⋆ (BS 63.1 vs 63.0; R-L is actually worse, 36.5 vs 36.9), and gains on QQP are within a narrow margin. No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for the seq2seq metrics; only MAUVE is averaged over 5 seeds. Given the number of moving parts (δ̃, d, steps, solver), some gains may not be robust.

Novelty is moderate: the method is essentially simplex diffusion with the trivial metric replaced by squared Euclidean distances, plus a self-conditioned architecture and noise schedule borrowed from prior work (TESS, TEncDM, Dieleman et al.). The strongest headline result (ROCStories, MAUVE 80.7 vs. TEncDM's 76.2) relies on careful tuning of δ̃, whose importance the paper itself shows is task-dependent, raising mild concern about cherry-picking sensitivity.

The practical significance of the diffusion-model contribution is limited by the fact that autoregressive baselines still clearly dominate on most metrics (e.g., FLAN-T5 and BART on XSum/QQP), so the work advances a niche (diffusion LM) rather than state-of-the-art text generation; the paper is upfront about this but its significance claims ('outperforms existing diffusion-based models') should be read in that light.

The claimed third contribution (the solver) is empirical only, tested under a modified forward process (Eq. 11) adapted solely to make DDPM/DDIM comparable, and the gains are described by the authors themselves as 'marginal'.
The code URL in the abstract is empty, which weakens reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameters in Appendix J.

No human evaluation is performed; all quality assessments rely on automatic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore/MAUVE/J-Score), which are imperfect proxies for generation quality, particularly for the fluency/diversity trade-off claims around δ̃.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: representing tokens by vectors of negative squared Euclidean distances to all vocabulary embeddings yields a diffusion space that both preserves a natural decoding path (via softmax over distances, like simplex diffusion) and incorporates semantic similarity (unlike simplex diffusion). The paper convincingly situates this as a generalization of simplex-based diffusion, with a correct and simple proof in Appendix A that the trivial metric recovers the simplex formulation.

The controlled comparison of latent spaces (Embedding*, Simplex*, SMOOTHIE*) under identical architecture, hyperparameters, and decoding strategy is a real strength; it isolates the contribution of the diffusion space rather than confounding it with engineering differences. The 1.75x step compensation for the faster embedding diffusion is a thoughtful fairness detail.

Evaluation coverage is broad: five datasets spanning unconditional and sequence-to-sequence generation, standard metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, MAUVE, perplexity, diversity, J-Score), and ablations of embeddings, noise scheduler, self-conditioning, denoising steps, and the solver choice.

The limitations section is honest and substantive (dependence on pre-trained BERT embeddings, difficulty of end-to-end embedding training, O(seq len x d x V) distance computation and why top-k approximation fails), which is more useful than the boilerplate typically found.

The variational-bound derivation and Theorem 4.1 (equivalence of predicting D0 vs. embeddings up to a constant shift) are correct as far as presented, and the qualitative degradation examples (Appendix L) support the semantic-smoothing claim.
weaknesses: The core technique is a relatively simple instantiation of an existing idea: Gaussian noise on a distance vector followed by a softmax is exactly a Nadaraya-Watson kernel smoother over embeddings, which the authors themselves note; the connection to blurring/heat-dissipation diffusion (Rissanen et al., 2023; Hoogeboom & Salimans, 2023) is acknowledged but the novelty over that line of work plus simplex diffusion is incremental. Table 1's 'we account for both discreteness and semantics' framing oversimplifies, since the model never actually operates on discrete tokens during diffusion.

Empirical gains over the strongest baselines are modest and inconsistent. SMOOTHIE* does not dominate its own Embedding* baseline: e.g., QQP BLEU 30.8 vs. 31.3, ROCStories diversity 25.1 vs. 26.1, Quasar-T where Simplex* matches it on BLEU and beats it on R-L. Much of the headline improvement (ROCStories MAUVE 80.7 vs. TEncDM 76.2) comes after tuning the generation-time hyperparameter delta-tilde per task, and no statistical significance tests or error bars (except averaging MAUVE over 5 seeds on one dataset) are provided, so several table entries are within noise.

The paper's comparison to external baselines mixes copied numbers, reproduced numbers, and re-implementations across different settings (e.g., TESS with/without RoBERTa initialization), which weakens the 'consistently outperforms existing text diffusion approaches' claim. The OpenWebText comparison also uses a hybrid solver (40% DDPM steps then Eq. 9) that is introduced only in the appendix and never justified in the main text.

The proposed solver (Eq. 9) is presented as a contribution, but it is essentially predicting x0 and re-noising with the forward process; the explanation for why it beats DDPM/DDIM is speculative ('sparse data distribution... drifting in incorrect directions') with no theoretical or empirical analysis beyond Table 6, where differences are small (e.g., 0.2-0.4 BERTScore points).

The forward process (Eq. 3) is non-Markovian and the reverse variance delta-tilde is decoupled from the forward noise, which means the learned model is not a principled posterior for the stated forward process; the variational-bound story (Eq. 6-7) glosses over this mismatch between the trained objective and the sampler.

Some presentation issues: typos ('lantert', 'minumum', 'AR-Diffsion', inconsistent 'other previous methods' in contributions), Figure 2 axis labels are hard to read, and the justification for delta-tilde = 0.1 on seq2seq tasks is relegated to a grid search over only five values on a single metric.
The claimed applicability to other categorical domains (graphs, proteins) is asserted but never tested, even on a toy setting.

strengths: The core idea is original and well-motivated: representing tokens as vectors of negative squared distances to all vocabulary embeddings yields a diffusion space that provably generalizes simplex diffusion (Appendix A) while injecting semantic structure into the noising process, drawing a principled connection to heat-dissipation/blurring diffusion in images (Rissanen et al., 2023).

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough and fair: embedding- and simplex-based baselines are re-implemented within the identical architecture, hyperparameters, and decoding strategy, so the comparison isolates the latent-space contribution; a wide range of diffusion and autoregressive baselines, five datasets, and multiple metrics are used.

Extensive ablations cover the noise scheduler (d), the reverse-noise hyperparameter δ̃, embedding choice (BERT vs GPT-2 vs GloVe), self-conditioning, number of denoising steps, and solver choice, and include useful analyses such as training-dynamics curves and semantic degradation examples.
The paper includes a clean theoretical result (Theorem 4.1) justifying the MSE-on-embeddings parameterization, with a correct and simple proof in Appendix C.

Limitations are discussed honestly and substantively: reliance on pre-trained (non-finetunable) embeddings, the O(V) distance-matrix bottleneck and why top-k approximations fail, and the unresolved theoretical question about the proposed solver.
A separate large-scale experiment on OpenWebText against GIDD strengthens the unconditional-generation claims beyond small benchmarks.
weaknesses: Headline improvements over the strongest controlled baseline (Embedding*) are small and inconsistent: e.g., XSum BS 68.8 vs 68.2, Quasar-T BLEU 19.9 vs 19.9 vs 18.9 (Simplex* ties/leads R-L), QQP R-L 60.9 vs 59.4, while Simplex* actually beats SMOOTHIE on D-1/4 for Quasar-T and BLEU on QQP/ParaDetox in places. No statistical significance tests, error bars, or variance across seeds are reported for these near-tie margins.

The claimed superiority of the proposed solver over DDPM/DDIM (Table 6) rests on differences of 0.2–0.4 BERTScore points without uncertainty quantification; the theoretical explanation is acknowledged as speculative ('hypothesize... remains an open question'), so this contribution rests on weak evidence.

The non-Markovian forward process with fixed δ and a reverse process with different variance (δ̃ ≠ δ) departs from standard diffusion ELBO assumptions; the variational-bound derivation (Appendix B) glosses over this mismatch, and the effect is handled empirically via grid search of δ̃ rather than theoretically justified.

The code link in the abstract is empty ('The code is available at .'), which undermines reproducibility claims; given the many tuned hyperparameters (δ̃, d per dataset, 1.75× step compensation for baselines), released code is important for verification.

Generative perplexity relies on GPT-2 as an external evaluator, which is known to favor outputs close to GPT-2's distribution; MAUVE results for baselines are absent or very low (e.g., DiffuSeq 8.6, Simplex* 15.2) partly because they are reproduced rather than tuned, complicating interpretation of the ROCStories gains.

The framing that the method 'combines strengths of both approaches' is somewhat overstated: the method still requires the softmax/argmax decoding machinery, and Table 1's dichotomy (Gaussian ignores discreteness) is a simplification of prior work.

Positioning relative to very recent masked/interpolating discrete diffusion (e.g., MDLM is compared, but the broader 2024–2026 discrete-diffusion literature, some of which is cited only in passing) is limited; it is unclear how SMOOTHIE would scale against modern masked diffusion LLMs at larger scales.
